easy.heading: Warming Up With The Basics
easy.body:
Solving the easy grid today was all about following the trail of clues Ian left for us. I started right at the top left where cell (0,0) had a target sum of 4. Since that cell was part of a horizontal domino, I knew it had to be either the [4,4] or the [4,6] from our list. The real breakthrough came when I looked at the equals constraint for (0,1) and (0,2). If I used the [4,6] domino for the first two cells, then (0,1) became 6, which forced (0,2) to also be 6. This was perfect because it allowed the next domino at (0,2) and (0,3) to be the [6,0] pair, fitting that empty region at (0,3) perfectly.

Down at the bottom, I had to deal with a sum of 3 across three cells: (4,0), (4,1), and (4,2). I noticed that (2,1) and (2,2) were tied together with an equals sign, and since they were one whole domino, they had to be a double. I used the [4,4] there, which left me with the [1,1] and [1,6] dominoes for the bottom row. By placing the [1,1] domino at (4,0) and (4,1), the sum was already at 2. That meant cell (4,2) had to be a 1 to hit our target of 3. It all clicked into place when I tucked the [1,6] domino into the final slot at (4,2) and (4,3).

medium.heading: Stepping Up To The Medium Grid
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt like a game of domino-effect logic, especially in the bottom half of the grid. I spent a good minute staring at the chain of equals signs connecting (3,1), (3,2), and (3,3). The key was the sum target of 4 at cell (3,4). Since (3,4) is part of a domino with (3,3), I realized that if I used the [5,4] domino there, it would set (3,3) to 5. This immediately filled that entire equals chain with 5s, which was a huge help.

Once those 5s were in, the rest of the board started to crumble. Cell (3,1) being a 5 meant the domino at (3,1) and (2,1) had to be the [2,5] pair. That set cell (2,1) to 2, and since it was equal to (1,1), that became a 2 as well. I then worked my way over to the far left where (1,0) and (2,0) had to sum to 7. By using the [2,2] domino at (1,1) and (1,0), I got a 2 for (1,0), which forced (2,0) to be a 5. This lined up perfectly with the [5,3] domino for the (3,0) and (2,0) spot, hitting our target sum of 2 for cell (3,0) after a little more shuffling.

hard.heading: Cracking The Kurchan Code
hard.body:
Rodolfo really made us work for it today! The biggest challenge on this hard grid was the high sum targets like the 10s at (1,3) and (2,3), and again at (4,0) and (4,1). In a game where the highest pip is a 5, the only way to hit a 10 across two cells is for both of them to be 5s. This was my breakthrough moment. I knew (4,0) and (4,1) both had to be 5, even though they belonged to different dominoes. By matching (4,0) with its neighbor (3,0), which had a target of 2, I successfully placed the [2,5] domino.

The top half of the grid was equally tight. I used the sum of 0 at (1,0) and (2,0) to place two dominoes starting with 0, which really narrowed down my options. The most satisfying part was solving the long chain around the (3,2), (3,3), and (3,4) equals constraint. Once I realized (2,3) had to be a 5 to help satisfy that vertical 10 sum, I could place the [4,5] domino at (3,3) and (2,3). This set the value for the entire equals chain to 4, and from there, the 0-sum regions at (1,4), (2,2), and (4,4) acted like anchors that held the whole solution together.

explanation.tips: When you see a target sum of 0, you know both cells must be the empty side of the domino. Also, always look for high sum targets like 9 or 10, as they usually force you to use 4s and 5s, which significantly limits your domino choices.
explanation.learned: I learned that high-value pips are often shared between neighboring sum regions to reach those double-digit targets. It was also interesting to see how a single equals chain can span across three different dominoes, creating a bottleneck that dictates the values for the entire bottom half of the board.

faqs.question: What does the empty region type mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region means there is no specific sum or equality constraint for that cell, so its value is determined entirely by the pips on the domino you place there.

faqs.question: How do you solve a sum target of 10 in Pips?
faqs.answer: Since the pips usually go up to 5 or 6, a target of 10 almost always requires two high-value pips like 5 and 5 or 4 and 6 from two different adjacent dominoes.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must be placed either horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent cells.

faqs.question: What is the best way to start a Hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Look for the most restrictive hints first, such as sum targets of 0, very high sum targets, or long chains of cells that must all be equal.

faqs.question: Are dominoes used more than once in a single puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, each domino from the provided list for that difficulty level is used exactly once in the grid.
